extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, IP lawyers, judges and practitioners managing orders to produce documents/materials in patent infringement cases (primarily Korea; comparative references to Japan, Germany, U.S.)
extracted.subtask_short: orders to produce materials in patent litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on scope, procedure, permissible objections, secrecy protections, and sanctions for court orders to produce materials (documents, electronic evidence, prototypes, goods) in patent infringement and damages proceedings. Emphasizes Korea's Amended Patent Act (Article 132) with comparative references to Japan, Germany, and the U.S.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production of bank documents and the like for a damages claim (German Patent Act Article 140d)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent holders can request the infringer’s “bank documents and the like” for the purpose of exercising the right to request damages. This requires infringement on a commercial scale, documents that are under the control of the infringer, and documents that meet the conditions of the request for damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines “bank documents and the like” to include bank documents, financial documents, and business documents. If the infringer requests preservation of secrecy, the court must take any action that may be required to protect confidentiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Japanese system for ordering production of documents (Article 105)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Article 105 of the Japanese Patent Act, the opposing party can be ordered to produce necessary documents 'in order to prove an infringement action or to calculate the damages resulting from such an infringement.' The possessor may be asked to set forth relevant documents and, where necessary, materials can be opened for examination to the relevant party, representative, and litigator/counselor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure contemplates specifying the examinations necessary for proving infringement and allows a possessor to present reasons for non-compliance; provides for limited participation and examination safeguards in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amended Act: subject change from 'written papers' to 'materials' (Article 132(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 132 Paragraph 1 of the Amended Act changes the subject of the order to produce from 'written papers' to 'materials' and adds the situation of 'proving the infringement' along with assessing losses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose is to allow collection of evidence in various forms not limited to written papers (e.g., electronic materials, drawings). The amendment explicitly broadens the statutory subject to include non-paper evidence to address difficulties proving infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of 'materials' subject to production
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'materials' includes everything subject to examination other than documents and also includes documents; there is potential inclusion of electronic data, videos, images, prototypes, goods, and other infringement-related items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While some precedents historically excluded videos/images, the Amended Act's purpose indicates videos/images are at least within the scope. Prototypes, manufacturing equipment, manufacturing processes and even materials that can be easily produced (e.g., filmed manufacturing videos) may be included. Comparative references: U.S. discovery includes electronic data, and Germany permits examination of goods and methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materials necessary to prove infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Orders to produce may cover materials 'necessary for proving the infringement,' including materials related to implemented products or implemented methods: parts necessary for the product, manufacturing equipment, manufacturing processes, and test results involving completed goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the Amended Act expanded orders to include proof of infringement, courts can order production of evidence tied to actual implementation and operation of accused products/methods; such materials are considered relevant and producible when needed to prove infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materials necessary to calculate damages and threshold to request them
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain materials necessary to calculate damages 'due to infringement,' the applicant must first prove that there is sufficient likelihood that infringement will be recognized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerated written papers relevant to damages calculation include: balance sheets, profit & loss statements, business reports, sales/purchase transaction ledgers, sales/purchase ledgers (statements), manufacturing cost reports, raw material ledgers, outbound sheets, product receipt/disbursement registers, inventory sheets, expense reports (manufacturing and sales), miscellaneous sales expenses directly incurred for the product, unit cost per sale, sales figures, manufacturing cost, and sale. Applicants should plead likelihood of infringement and specify entries/documents sought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application contents for an order to produce materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying for production requires a written application that includes a description of the documents/materials and their purpose, the possessor, the facts to be proven, and the reasons for the duty to produce the documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civil Procedure Act provisions (Article 345, Article 110(1), Article 346) apply by analogy: the court may require the applicant to identify the descriptions/aims of the documents and the possessor. Specificity in describing entries sought is important but courts recognize practical difficulty when opposing party possesses materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content of an order where trade secrets are implicated (Article 132(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: If the subject of the order to produce falls under the category of a trade secret, the court must 'specify what is accessible within the bounds of the purpose of the order to produce or specify an entity that is allowed access.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice access is likely limited to persons subject to a secrecy order (e.g., counsel, experts). The statute contemplates tailoring access (what is viewable and by whom) to protect trade secrets while allowing necessary evidence inspection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate (valid) reasons for non-compliance with an order to produce
rubrics_metrics.description: The Amended Act defines non-compliance excuses as a general/abstract 'appropriate reason' but does not enumerate them. Trade secrets are not an automatic appropriate reason when the materials are 'absolutely necessary to prove infringement or calculate damages.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Views differ on whether appropriate reasons should mirror Civil Procedure Act enumerated grounds or be more limited. Because the Amended Act expands production scope to remedy evidentiary maldistribution, acceptable reasons for non-compliance should be rare and limited—determined by weighing the possessor's hardship from disclosure (e.g., irreparable business harm) against the applicant's need and trial fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure and safeguards for examining asserted reasons (in-camera examination)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the possessor argues an appropriate reason not to produce, the court can order production for private examination (in camera) to determine whether the argument is accepted; in such cases the court must not allow any other entity to view the materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is debate whether the applicant (or applicant’s representatives such as public accountants) may participate in the in-camera procedure; some viewpoints exclude applicants to protect secrets, others permit restricted representatives or appraisers. Korean, Japanese and comparative practice recognizes the use of in-camera review and appraisers to resolve disputes while limiting third-party exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participation limits and use of appraisers/experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Orders to produce materials are limited to the parties of the action (not third parties), and when the court cannot itself evaluate trade secret claims it may choose an appraiser and allow limited participation by that appraiser.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical considerations include whether the applicant’s counsel/representatives should be excluded from in-camera review to avoid irreversible disclosure; courts may allow participation by neutral appraisers or restricted access to nominated experts under secrecy orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions for non-compliance with an order to produce (Articles 132(4) and 132(5))
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 132(4) allows the court, if a party does not comply without an appropriate reason, to 'acknowledge as fact the opposing party’s arguments regarding the materials in question.' Article 132(5) further permits the court to acknowledge as fact the argued facts to be proven by the documents when the applicant cannot specify entries and cannot rely on other evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court distinguishes between acknowledging the nature/contents/validity of documents as fact and acknowledging the substantive factual claims those documents would prove; under (5) the court may take the more decisive step of treating the argued facts as established where the applicant truly lacks alternative proof. These provisions were adopted to provide meaningful penalties given criticism that prior sanctions were insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance test for deciding appropriate reasons (weighing test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a reason is appropriate is determined by weighing the difficulties borne by the possessor if secrets are exposed against the difficulties and trial fairness burdens the applicant faces from non-production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts consider multiple variables: content and form of information, degree to which information is needed as evidence, effect of submission on possessor’s business, and the applicant’s discovery/trial fairness hardships. Acceptable reasons are limited to cases where protecting secrecy is worth sacrificing the request to discover facts (rare).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation of orders to produce to parties and treatment of third-party orders
rubrics_metrics.description: Orders to produce materials as discussed are limited to parties to the action; orders to produce documents that implicate third parties raise distinct practical and participation concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because orders to produce materials are party-limited, procedures for third-party production (and their protections) differ; courts may treat third-party requests with heightened scrutiny for secrecy and participation safeguards.
